Frank Mautino speaks with reporters on the House floor in Springfield in January 2011.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>But Pietro Mautino’s case highlights the political ties of the Special Prosecution Unit’s leaders, who at times have their own conflicts of interest and political entanglements.</p><p>Before Pietro Mautino’s arrest, the Illinois State’s Attorney’s Association PAC, a political action committee that shared an address and leadership with the Special Prosecution Unit, made contributions to Frank Mautino’s campaign. Soon after, Mautino became the state auditor general, one of the few state officials with even nominal oversight over the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>The state agency housing the Special Prosecution Unit has long handed out no-bid contracts to political insiders and hired well-connected prosecutors, government records show. And the unit has shielded defendants with clout while its political allies helped protect the agency from public scrutiny by writing it out of the state’s public records law.</p><p>The charges against Pietro Mautino stalled for three years before a special prosecutor offered a plea deal that enabled him to avoid prison. Under the deal, he was sentenced to 24 months of special probation before the public case file was expunged, according to court records and news reports.</p><p>The special prosecutor handling the case, Dave Neal, explained the trial delays by saying police drug-testing labs had a backlog of more serious cases. A police report from downstate Peru shows lab testing was not conducted until 2017, more than two years into the prosecution. But the officer who handled the test says he would have done so sooner if asked by the prosecutor. Neal did not respond to requests for comment.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-9a0000" name="image-9a0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/36ae72a/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d3f91f6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45fb191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lake County Special Prosecutor Dave Neal talks to a witness during the sentencing hearing for Daniel Baker at the Lake County courthouse in Waukegan Monday for the murder of 50-year-old Marina Aksman in her Vernon Hills home on April1, 2010. Baker was sentenced by Lake County Judge Daniel B. Shanes after he was found guilty but mentally ill in November 2012. | Pool/Daily Herald, Gilbert Boucher ORG XMIT: 31919_" srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45fb191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/02a350f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/45fb191/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2400x1347+0+173/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F71%2F79%2F4c646ba24ba2948bcaab0a82bd49%2Fbaker-lcn-043013-6.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Special prosecutor Dave Neal talks to a witness during a sentencing hearing in April 2013 for Daniel Baker, who was found guilty but mentally ill in the murder of Marina Aksman at her Vernon Hills home.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Daily Herald</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The local prosecutor who initially fielded Pietro Mautino’s case but then referred it to the unit — LaSalle County State’s Attorney Brian Towne — joined the unit two years later, highlighting the often close relationships between the Special Prosecution Unit and the local prosecutors they’re brought in to replace. Frank Mautino had donated more than $5,500 to Towne’s campaigns in the years before his son’s prosecution, campaign finance data show, and news reports show Towne honored Mautino with an Outstanding Legislator Award in 2015.</p><h3><b>An agency hidden from public view</b></h3><p>The unit’s parent agency, the Illinois State’s Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor, or ILSAAP, was created in 1977 to help local prosecutors fight a flood of appeals from indigent prisoners. At the time, Illinois courts were expanding the rights of people who contested their convictions and lawmakers had created the Office of the State Appellate Defender to represent them. County state’s attorneys and their legislative allies created ILSAAP as a counterforce.</p><p>ILSAAP’s mission statement, then and now, is spelled out in its annual reports: “Keep convicted criminals behind bars.”</p><p>ILSAAP’s power has been expanded steadily over the past four decades as state lawmakers added a slew of new legal assignments to its now-$36 million annual budget: assisting state’s attorneys with property tax cases, helping distribute drug forfeiture funds, training county prosecutors on the Pretrial Fairness Act and other laws — and deploying special prosecutors when local officials have a conflict of interest.</p><p>But ILSAAP’s oversight structure creates an apparent conflict of interest that shadows the Special Prosecution Unit’s work.</p><p>The “independent” special prosecutors are governed by a board of 10 elected state’s attorneys who rely on ILSAAP to defend them on appeals and replace them with special prosecutors when they or their offices have a conflict.</p><p>The board establishes the agency’s rules, regulations and procedures, and governs all aspects of ILSAAP’s operation, agency publications say. But the public minutes from recent meetings show only the barest oversight; the March 2026 meeting lasted just seven minutes.</p><p>That’s about the only scrutiny the agency gets.</p><p>In 2010, as ILSAAP was facing public records requests about the Special Prosecution Unit, ILSAAP leaders pulled off a legislative sleight of hand to shield themselves from public view.</p><p>ILSAAP was initially formed as a commission within Illinois’ executive branch, making it subject to the Freedom of Information Act, which requires government agencies to provide documents and information to the public upon request.</p><p>But then-state Sen. William Haine, a former Madison County state’s attorney who served as ILSAAP’s point person in the General Assembly, quietly introduced a bill making ILSAAP part of the judicial branch, which is exempt from FOIA in Illinois.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c90000" name="image-c90000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/f4468a6/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/9dab4d1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/21807ae/2147483647/strip/true/crop/2976x1670+0+345/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2Fb1%2F1195b4d94e3eb0398f6dc78e083d%2Fmedical-marijuana-llinois.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois Sen. William Haine is congratulated after his medical marijuana legislation passed on the Senate floor in May 2013.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>AP file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>On the Senate floor, when Haine introduced the bill, he did not explain to fellow lawmakers that he was doing so to make ILSAAP exempt from public records laws. He never even used words like “judicial” or “FOIA,”, legislative transcripts show.</p><p>Instead, Haine told fellow lawmakers he was making an “update” that “allows for a different configuration in the board and a few other things that updates the office.”</p><p>When ILSAAP’s exemption from FOIA was later debated in court in 2013, the Illinois’ Appellate Court ridiculed ILSAAP’s new designation as an arm of the state courts. Calling ILSAAP a judicial agency was like saying a dog had five legs because you counted its tail as one leg, the court wrote in Uphoff v. Grosskopf, citing a quip from Abraham Lincoln.</p><p>ILSAAP “is, in fact, in no sense a judicial agency of state government,” the court wrote. The legislative intent of Haine’s bill was simple: “to provide a FOIA exemption for that agency.”</p><p>Yet because of Haine’s change in the law, the court wrote, it had no choice but to uphold ILSAAP’s exemption from public records laws.</p><p>The maneuver deprives Illinois citizens of their basic right to be informed about the workings of a critical government agency, says Steve Helle, a professor emeritus of journalism at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a secrecy, but they disdain the public they profess to serve if they do not resist the temptation,” Helle says.</p><p>Haine retired from the legislature in 2019 and died two years later. Today, ILSAAP is still part of the judiciary on paper, but the state Supreme Court provides no oversight or even interaction with ILSAAP or the Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>“There’s nothing in the Illinois State’s Attorneys Appellate Prosecutors Act that requires the [Administrative Office of the Illinois Courts] or Supreme Court to provide oversight,” says Illinois courts spokesperson Christopher Bonjean.</p><p>ILSAAP Director Patrick Delfino and Board Chair Ben Goetten did not respond to requests for comment.</p><h3><b>Political contributions and no-bid contracts</b></h3><p>ILSAAP has had just two directors in the past 35 years.</p><p>Former Greene County State’s Attorney Norbert Goetten took over the agency in 1991. He was succeeded in 2008 by his top aide, Patrick Delfino, a former director of planning and special projects for the Cook County state’s attorney’s office who helped write the legislation that created ILSAAP.</p><p>Both were accused of misconduct in the 1990s, when then-state Auditor General William Holland scrutinized ILSAAP’s use of contracts and state phones. Holland reported in a public audit that ILSAAP no-bid contractors were being paid with little evidence they did any actual work, and ILSAAP staffers were using their state phones to make personal long-distance calls.</p><p>Delfino agreed to give up an accumulated 55 vacation days to pay for private calls allegedly made on a state phone, including calls to a girlfriend, the State Journal-Register reported in 1995. Goetten said at the time that the 55 days amounted to “way more” than the cost of Delfino’s personal phone calls.</p><p>ILSAAP contract records were subpoenaed by the U.S. attorney’s office, with the FBI interviewing Goetten, the State Journal-Register reported, but no charges were filed.</p><p>Goetten survived the scrutiny by the auditor general and the FBI, and he and his family deepened their ties to ILSAAP.</p><p>His son, Jersey County State’s Attorney Ben Goetten, has served as chairman of ILSAAP’s Board of Governors since 2020. Another son, Matthew Goetten, is an ILSAAP special prosecutor, while Goetten’s grandson, Connor Goetten, is an ILSAAP staff attorney.</p><p>Norbert Goetten ran a private Jersey County law practice while running ILSAAP. He was chair of ILSAAP’s political action committee and contributed more than $10,000 of his own money to Illinois politicians.</p><p>His son Ben was later treasurer of the PAC, which began making political donations to legislative allies while Goetten was in charge of ILSAAP. From 2006 to 2015, the PAC donated $6,200 to Haine, who sponsored the legislation exempting ILSAAP from FOIA.</p><p>ILSAAP continues to award no-bid consulting and legal services contracts to political insiders and lawyers with spotty records. ILSAAP and the contractors declined to comment.</p><p>In the most recent fiscal year, the agency awarded no-bid contracts to Lisa Duarte, a former top aide to Gov. JB Pritzker, and her firm worth up to $146,000. Former 5th Ward Chicago Ald. Leslie Hairston was awarded a contract worth $81,000 and former 6th Ward Ald. Borges Jr., has twice been censured by the Illinois Supreme Court, once for failing to pay income taxes and once for failure to diligently represent two clients.</p><p>Former Lake County Chief Deputy State’s Attorney Jeffrey Pavletic also holds a no-bid legal consulting contract. The Chicago Tribune reported in 2012 on Pavletic’s “spate of collapsing prosecutions in Lake County, including high-profile cases that disintegrated in the face of contradictory evidence.”</p><p>One such case was that of Juan Rivera, whom Pavletic prosecuted for the 1992 rape and murder of 11-year-old Holly Staker in Waukegan. Rivera, who was 19 at the time, was found guilty in three separate trials on the basis of a confession that followed a four-day interrogation. DNA evidence tying another man to the crime helped clear Rivera in 2011, after he had spent 20 years in prison. He later received a certificate of innocence and won a $20 million settlement.</p><p>Other states have found ways to protect against some of the controversies surrounding Illinois’ special prosecutors, according to an analysis of statutes and court decisions, law review articles, and news reports from all 50 states.</p><p>In Maryland, for example, the governor must appoint a new state prosecutor every six years, or reappoint the current one. Applicants are vetted by a seven-member commission of judges, lawyers, and former lawmakers, says Maryland Deputy State Prosecutor Sarah David.</p><p>“I think that is really important, because there's more community buy-in on the front end,” she says.</p><p>To read the full Injustice Watch series, please go <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/projects/shadow-prosecutors/" entries.title: Clout, conflicts of interest cloud the work of Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit
entries.summary: <p>The former assistant state’s attorney charged with murder.</p><p>The judge caught driving drunk.</p><p>The clerk accused of skimming government funds.</p><p>When local prosecutors might have political or personal ties to a defendant, the state brings in an elite squad of government attorneys: the Illinois Special Prosecution Unit.</p><p>They are supposed to be lawyers beyond reproach.</p><p>Instead, the unit has been clouded by allegations of corruption, misconduct and conflicts of interest.</p><p>The two dozen lawyers of Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit are mostly former county state’s attorneys, many with powerful political connections. All are white, most are men.</p><p>Since its creation in the 1980s, the unit has been the primary way criminal cases in Illinois are handled when local state’s attorneys are disqualified because of conflicts. Its prosecutors took on more than 1,000 cases in 2024, far more than were pursued through other methods of appointing special prosecutors, including referrals to the state attorney general, private attorneys or prosecutors from neighboring counties.</p><p>But the Special Prosecution Unit has been responsible for miscarriages of justice including withholding evidence and favorable treatment of political insiders, as well as conflicts of interest and ethical breaches.</p><p>To examine the Special Prosecution Unit, Injustice Watch reviewed thousands of pages of court documents and interviewed dozens of people, including defendants who were wrongly charged, victims who never saw justice, unit veterans and legal experts.</p><p>Here are the key findings:<br></p><ul class="rte2-style-ul" id="rte-c2a08352-9716-11f1-978c-7f7413ccaf70"><li>Special prosecutors withheld exculpatory evidence that could have set murder defendant Curtis Lovelace free. The former Adams County prosecutor was acquitted in 2017 for the murder of his wife after spending 21 months in jail, but the misguided prosecution <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/prosecutorial-misconduct-curtis-lovelace/" target="_blank" >tore through his community and life</a>. </li><li>In 2014, special prosecutors were called in after police arrested the son of Frank Mautino, who had represented LaSalle County for nearly a quarter-century as a state lawmaker. A political action committee tied to the Special Prosecution Unit made donations to Mautino’s campaign fund and <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/political-ties-little-oversight/" target="_blank" >supported his appointment as state auditor general</a>, one the of the few state offices with a limited watchdog function over the unit. </li><li>After 31-year-old mother of three Megan Wells was killed in a 2016 Rock River boat crash by an allegedly drunk boater, special prosecutors dropped most of the charges as part of a plea deal, <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/project/shadow-prosecutors/2026/conflicts-of-interest-powerful-defendants/" target="_blank" >allowing the defendant, a well-connected pharmacist, to walk free</a>. The lead prosecutor never publicly disclosed a professional connection to the local state’s attorney he replaced.</li></ul><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-720000" name="image-720000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ac9be93/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/d0a553f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/056c713/2147483647/strip/true/crop/5520x3098+0+291/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F83%2Fc9%2F99ad70b54bc1b283629e0a85583d%2Feonri-cst-071714-2.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Rep. Frank Mautino, right, speaks during a Legislative Audit Commission hearing in July 2014.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In other cases, the Special Prosecution Unit seemed to go after low-level political scapegoats, failing to secure convictions, but leaving devastation in its wake.</p><p>In 2007, special prosecutors filed four felony charges against McLean County Clerk Peggy Ann Milton for allegedly misusing a roll of postage stamps to support a charity and asking a county employee to drive her son home on county time. The jury quickly acquitted Milton, but her life was upended.</p><p>“My son was young at the time, and [the prosecutor] intimidated him,” Milton says. "Once something like that is so public, especially in a small community, it's difficult for you to get past it.”</p><p>The special prosecutors responsible for these and other questionable cases all remain on the job today. Others were hired by the Special Prosecution Unit despite alleged impropriety in their past roles.</p><p>William Elward joined the Special Prosecution Unit after a 2016 state inspector general's report found he submitted false time sheets while working for the Illinois attorney general’s office, improperly billing the state for hundreds of hours when he was in fact moonlighting as a law teacher out of state.</p><p>Another special prosecutor, Brian Towne, was criminally charged after he joined the unit with misappropriating money confiscated by a rogue unit he created as LaSalle County state’s attorney to seize assets during traffic stops. The charges were dropped under speedy trial rules as Towne fought the case, which he claimed was retribution from a political rival.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Verónica Martinez/Injustice Watch</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Elward and Towne did not respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The Special Prosecution Unit is housed in an obscure, insular state agency, the Office of the Illinois State's Attorneys Appellate Prosecutor, or ILSAAP, which operates with little oversight.</p><p>ILSAAP has had just two directors over the past 35 years, including one whose two sons and grandson have held key positions in the office. The agency is exempt from the state Freedom of Information Act, not scrutinized by any inspector general and does not answer to the governor or the state attorney general.</p><p>Illinois is an outlier among states in having a unit of special prosecutors who try local government corruption cases without meaningful oversight from any elected official.</p><p>The board that governs the agency is made up of state’s attorneys from across Illinois — the very same officials who call on the special prosecutors to step in when they or their offices have a conflict of interest. But even they provide only superficial oversight, holding only brief periodic meetings.</p><p>And although ILSAAP was created to assist downstate prosecutors, its authority has expanded into Cook County criminal courts.</p><p>ILSAAP reviews every police-involved fatal shooting in Cook County when the state’s attorney declines charges, making an independent determination of whether charges against the officer are appropriate.</p><p>As of last year, ILSAAP had conducted 73 such reviews since 2016 and never overruled the Cook County state’s attorney’s decision not to charge, records show.</p><p>ILSAAP Director Patrick Delfino declined to comment. While the agency said it strives to be transparent, and Delfino provided basic data on cases the unit handled in 2024, he did not respond to detailed written questions.</p><p>Injustice Watch’s review found cases where special prosecutors obtained convictions and followed the law. Several attorneys in the unit have been praised for their work in underserved rural counties, including special prosecutors who have appeared in courts across the state to bring people charged with child sexual abuse to trial.</p><p>The unit as a whole handled a small fraction of the nearly 240,000 criminal cases filed statewide in 2024, and the wide range in the number and types of cases managed by Illinois’ more than 100 county prosecutors prevents any apples-to-apples comparison between the Special Prosecution Unit and local state’s attorney’s offices.</p><p>Yet unlike local prosecutors, Illinois’ Special Prosecution Unit is not answerable to any one elected official, so there is little if any responsibility for patterns of civil rights violations and unjust outcomes.</p><p>"There's been a number of cases against innocent people brought by the special prosecutors,” says private investigator Bill Clutter, who helped clear four defendants wrongly accused of murder by the group.</p><p>“They’ve just been on the wrong side of justice,” he says.</p><p>To read the full Injustice Watch series, please go <a class="Link" href="https://www.injusticewatch.org/projects/shadow-prosecutors/" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Funeral home shocker, pollution, mad bomber: Far South Side neighbors have been through a lot
entries.summary: <p>Jim Kinney has seen just about everything in his Far Southeast Side neighborhood: industrial waste that lit up the sky, the crime of the century, a mad bomber and a business that’s been allowed to fill the air with a stench that smells like rotting flesh.</p><p>Recently, just across the alley from his longtime home on 95th Street near Commercial Avenue, it was discovered that a funeral parlor neglected to care for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/06/decomposing-bodies-found-funeral-home-south-chicago-chapel-95th-street" >dozens of dead bodies</a> that were in various stages of decomposing.</p><p>“You can’t enjoy any outdoor things in the summer,” he says. “It smells like something died.”</p><p>Kinney is not describing South Chicago Chapel funeral home just behind his house, which was recently closed after the discovery of rotting bodies. He’s detailing a longtime nuisance that plagued the Far Southeast Side for decades: a feed-additive plant now operated by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" >Pullman Innovations</a>, which is being sued by residents and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/08/05/attorney-general-city-lawsuit-against-pullman-innovations-odors-kwame-raoul" >city and state authorities</a>.</p><p>This is the community of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/south-deering" >South Deering</a>, or as locals know it, Vet’s Park or Slag Valley — a nickname with roots in the steel-making heyday of Chicago. Decades ago, companies dumped molten metal left over from steelmaking into sites across the neighborhood. The waste product is known as slag, which is still prevalent throughout the area.</p><p>“We’d see the whole sky light up like a volcano,” Kinney says.</p><p>The 74-year-old Kinney, his dad and his grandfather all worked in the nearby mills, which mostly closed by the 1980s. There was Wisconsin Steel just to the south and U.S. Steel north of the home where he grew up along with 16 family members. You can’t talk about the Southeast Side without noting the legacy of the steel mills.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-430000" name="html-embed-module-430000"></a><div style="min-height:617px" id="datawrapper-vis-3kV22"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3kV22/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-3kV22"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/3kV22/full.png" alt="Smells around South Deering (Locator map)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Only about 20% of the larger South Deering neighborhood, which stretches from 95th Street on the north to 130th Street south, is residential. The remaining parts are industrial land, brownfields, wetlands or land reclaimed after the steel industry all but destroyed much of it decades ago.</p><p>The Slag Valley neighborhood and nearby Jeffrey Manor were also rocked by some of the most brutal crimes of the 20th century. Mass murderer Richard Speck killed eight student nurses in 1966 just a little more than a mile southwest of the funeral home.</p><p>In 1969, Frank Kulak, who lived across the back alley from Kinney’s family home, was arrested after a shootout with police that killed two officers. Kulak had planted homemade bombs across the Southeast Side, killing and injuring multiple people over a 20-month period.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> She says smells from Pullman Innovations, remind her of a foul garbage stench. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Pullman officials didn't respond to requests for comment.</p><p>“It’s been a problem in the neighborhood for some time,” says Ramon Valles, who lives up the street from Martin, “for as long as I can remember.”</p><p>Asked this week how the smell of dead bodies went unnoticed at the South Chicago Chapel funeral home at 2939 E. 95th St., Ald. Peter Chico said his office gets many complaints about foul smells.</p><p>“The stench from Pullman was so strong and putrid that the funeral home never came up,” Chico says.</p><p>Some residents have had enough.</p><p>“I’d like to see them close,” says Peggy Salazar, referring to Pullman.</p><p>Salazar, now retired, led environmental fights against Pullman and other polluting businesses, including a plan for the General Iron scrap metal operation in nearby East Side and large stockpiles of toxic materials.</p><p>It still has longtime residents. The area around South Chicago Chapel counts seniors as almost a third of the population. The area around the chapel is largely Latino, though more than 60% of South Deering is Black, census data show.</p><p>The area was the site of legal and illegal dumps. It has two active Superfund sites. The Calumet River, used primarily for commercial purposes, can stink. Residents fought and won city laws that provided tougher oversight of heaps of pet coke, manganese and other harmful materials that blew across the Southeast Side.</p><p>Pullman refines vegetable oils for use in chicken feed at farms that source eggs for the Dutch Farms brand.</p><p>The city has received numerous complaints over the years about odor from Pullman and a predecessor operator at the site known as Agri-Fine. Neighbors battled Agri-Fine for more than 20 years until it declared for bankruptcy protection more than a decade ago. Pullman was established in 2015.</p><p>Pullman Innovations, 2701 E. 100th St., is roughly a mile from the funeral home. Yet wind direction can push the smell throughout the larger South Deering area.</p><p>“People are desensitized by smells,” says Anna Johnson, who lives in Jeffrey Manor closer to the Pullman plant. entries.title: Chicago Sinfonietta musicians have a new one-year deal, but performances are still paused
entries.summary: <p>Amid a trying moment for the local orchestra, the Chicago Sinfonietta and the players’ union, the Chicago Federation of Musicians, have agreed to a new, one-year contract.</p><p>But that contract, announced Thursday, arrives with only one performance on the horizon as <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/07/chicago-sinfonietta-layoff-program-pause-finance-classical-music-2027" target="_blank" ><u>the Sinfonietta has abruptly halted concerts and educational programming</u></a> and laid off administrative staff. The nearly 40-year-old group is known for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/classical-music/2026/05/08/chicago-sinfonietta-pause-financial-trouble-musicians-reaction-shock-diversity-classical" target="_blank" ><u>championing diverse musicians and composers</u></a>.</p><p>The players’ current three-year labor agreement was set to expire at the end of this month, and renewal was uncertain, given the Sinfonietta’s abrupt pause that started in the spring. Management calls it a “strategic renewal period” to focus on fundraising and sustainability planning.</p><p>“The agreement continues the long-standing collaborative labor relationship between the [Chicago Federation of Musicians] and the Chicago Sinfonietta, ensuring that a collective bargaining framework remains in place as the organization works to strengthen its financial foundation and chart its next chapter,” the union said in a statement.</p><p>BJ Levy, president of Chicago Federation of Musicians, Local 10-208 of the American Federation of Musicians, said Thursday that management bargained in good faith to reach the agreement, which includes a cost-of-living increase. “We’re pleased that we were able to get wage gains in this one-year period,” Levy said.</p><p>However, the 63 rostered musicians only get paid when they perform, which they haven’t done with the Sinfonietta since May.</p><p>The new agreement currently includes only one upcoming concert, to be held in January, in alignment with Martin Luther King Jr. Day and the group’s 40th anniversary. The Sinfonietta previously said it plans to present a fundraising event tied to MLK Day. However, the union noted Thursday that the concert has yet to be scheduled.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Sidney Jackson, Sinfonietta’s president and CEO said in a statement Thursday, “The Chicago Sinfonietta Board is pleased to have reached a short-term agreement with the Chicago Federation of Musicians. This will allow us time and flexibility to develop a longer-term plan to achieve programmatic success and financial sustainability.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Manuel Martinez/Manuel Martinez/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Sidney Jackson was appointed to lead the orchestra in 2025 and, after the spring’s layoffs, became the organization’s only full-time employee.</p><p>“The Chicago Sinfonietta Board is pleased to have reached a short-term agreement with the Chicago Federation of Musicians,” Jackson said in a statement Thursday. “This will allow us time and flexibility to develop a longer-term plan to achieve programmatic success and financial sustainability.”</p><p>“The Board of Directors and I are continuing to work through our strategic renewal plans for the coming season, including our approach around MLK. We don’t have additional details to share at this time, but we look forward to sharing more when our plans are finalized.”</p><p>In its decision to halt operations, the Sinfonietta cited financial hardships brought on by the COVID-19 pandemic. In a statement on its website, the group said, “The pandemic fundamentally changed audience behavior across the performing arts sector, and Chicago Sinfonietta was not immune.”</p><p>“Like many arts organizations, our audience numbers and contributions have not returned to pre-COVID levels. Over that same period, an overreliance on grant funding meant that other revenue streams weren’t developed enough to sustain the organization once those grants ran out,” the statement reads.</p><div city’s Department of Cultural Affairs and Special Events between 2019 and 2025. Additionally, the group received $245,000 in grants from the National Endowment for the Arts from 2019 to 2024 for new commissions, performances and educational activities.</p><p>In recent years, under the Trump administration, the NEA — the nation’s preeminent arts funder — has canceled grants to organizations, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/05/06/nea-grants-trump-chicago-cultural-event" target="_blank" ><u>including some in Chicago</u></a>, and <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/arts-culture/2025/02/14/trump-nea-grants-national-endowment-arts-chicago-theater-dance" target="_blank" ><u>changed its grantmaking priorities</u></a>, with a prohibition on using federal monies for programs supporting “diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) that violate any applicable federal anti-discrimination laws.”</p><p>Levy said those changes at the federal level present a particular concern for Sinfonietta players and the future of the orchestra, founded by distinguished Black conductor Paul Freeman.</p><p>“It was quite unique in that Maestro Freeman founded the orchestra and was an African American conductor of great note, so that's what we're particularly concerned about,” Levy said. “In light of the federal government's outright attack on organizations that have a policy that is intended to promote underrepresented classes and include diversity, equity, inclusion in their mission statements.”</p><p>The union said it has received a commitment from the Sinfonietta to return to the table in March to negotiate for a new, three-year contract. The one-year deal is set to expire at the end of August 2027.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ.</i></p>

entries.title: Bat tests positive for rabies in Oak Lawn
entries.summary: <p>A bat tested positive for rabies in Oak Lawn, Cook County officials announced. </p><p>The bat was found in the 9800 block of South Pulaski Road, officials announced Thursday. </p><p>Pet owners are encouraged to stay up to date on vaccinations and the Cook County Animal and Rabies Control is hosting free rabies and microchips clinics through October to keep pets protected. </p><p>More information on the clinics can be found <a class="Link" href="https://www.cookcountyil.gov/service/low-cost-rabies-clinic" target="_blank" >here</a>. </p>

entries.title: Earle Johnson, beer pioneer and welcoming owner of Quenchers tavern, dies at 83
entries.summary: <p></p><p></p><p></p><p>As the owner of Quenchers, one of the city's first destination beer bars, Earle Johnson tapped into the power of nostalgia to draw customers.</p><p>Mr. Johnson stocked beer from nearly every country imaginable; when people returned from vacation — say in Argentina — and wanted to tap into the memory of drinking a beer on the beach, they could head to Quenchers in Logan Square and find that particular brew.</p><p>"I don't know how he did it. It was a lot of work carrying a beer that one person in 10,000 was interested in, but he was really good at creating his own niche market and a truly unique place, a place that people would go way out of their way for," said Michael Roeper, a friend who owns Hopleaf Bar.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Quenchers tavern, at 2401 N. Western Ave., in 2003. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Brian Jackson/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Mr. Johnson, who took ownership of the bar in 1981, was a beer pioneer decades before the microbrew craze swept the city and country.</p><p>"He was really, really ahead of the curve," Roeper said.</p><p>After putting 39 years of his life into Quenchers, at Fullerton and Western, the tavern closed in 2018. </p><p>Mr. Johnson, then 75, felt it was time, and sold the building. </p><p>A medical clinic is now where the bar used to be. </p><p>The space, prior to World War II, was an ice cream parlor. After the war it was turned into a bar and liquor store named Jug Full Liquors.</p><p>Mr. Johnson felt lucky to have sold two years before the pandemic hit the bar industry hard.</p><p>In retirement he read, traveled (including to Antarctica), spent time with his wife and two sons, and in recent months was putting the finishing touches on his dream home on the Northwest Side, but unfortunately never had the opportunity to move in.</p><p>Mr. Johnson died Aug. 4 following a heart attack. He was 83.</p><p>It's a wonder he ended up as a saloon keeper. His prior career trajectory was in Christian ministry.</p><p>Raised in Waukon, Iowa, a small town in the northeast corner of the state, Mr. Johnson attended Wheaton College, earned a master's degree from McCormick Theological Seminary and for several years worked in underserved Chicago communities as an outreach minister for Youth for Christ.</p><p>He shifted his focus to hospitality in his 30s after working at several restaurants, including The Berghoff in the Loop.</p><p>In 1979 he found himself bartending at Quenchers. Within months he became an investor and two years later owned the bar and building outright.</p><p>The bar was in a working class Polish and Hispanic area facing gentrification concerns, but Mr. Johnson made it clear that, in addition to welcoming traveling beer nerds, his place was a friendly neighborhood tavern.</p><p>It accrued regulars who had bar nicknames based on the simplest things about them, like "Old Man Bill." Another guy known as Whitey (the origin of the moniker is lost to time) folded the dollar bills he left on the bar as tips into origami animals.</p><p>"People felt at home there," said Cindy Weisbecker, a former patron and bartender who married another Quenchers bartender.</p><p>"I had a girl friend who'd stop there in the afternoon and balance her checkbook and just sit there have a coke because she knew it'd be a safe place where no would harass her, and that tone was set by Earle," she said.</p><p>"That's how I met Earle, he made me feel comfortable while I was at the bar waiting for my brother," said his wife, Nisa Johnson. "I brought up football, and no man could refuse to talk about football."</p><p>Scuffed wood, tin ceilings and old-fashioned glass-paneled cooler doors with latches that clicked shut provided ambiance. </p><p>"It was a place where a millionaire might be sitting next to some guy who just got out of jail, and the two could be talking and having a nice conversation," said David Weisbecker, who bartended there in the '80s.</p><p>In his younger days, if the mood struck, Mr. Johnson was known to perform somersaults down the length of the bar.</p><p>Though his work in Christian ministry never led him to head up a church, Mr. Johnson liked to say "This bar is my mission now, with a flock of a different kind."</p><p>He was a familiar and welcoming face to homeless people and others on the fringe of society who could depend on Mr. Johnson for a few bucks, a glass of orange juice, a working telephone and a safe place to sit for a while.</p><p>"He had a lot of empathy for people, especially people facing challenges, and he wanted to make people feel welcome and not out in the wilderness on their own," his wife said.</p><p>He was a longtime member of the Church of the Three Crosses in Old Town.</p><p>Quenchers was also known for its annual European Beer Tour, an event where Mr. Johnson issued "passports" complete with Polaroid photos that would be stamped at "Checkpoint Earle" after sampling beers from various countries.</p><p>There was also the Walk to Wrigley, in which dozens of people set off on foot from Quenchers on a pub crawl ending at the ballpark to take in a Cubs game.</p><p>An honorary street sign reading "Earle Johnson Way" was placed outside the bar before it closed.</p><p>In addition to his wife, Mr. Johnson is survived by his sons David Johnson and Dean Johnson.</p><p>A visitation will take place on Aug. 15 from 10 a.m. to noon at the Church of the Three Crosses, 333 W. Wisconsin St., in Old Town. It will be immediately followed by a funeral service from noon to 1:30 p.m.</p>

entries.title: 3 hurt in fiery Gold Coast wreck along North DuSable LSD
entries.summary: <p>Three people were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital after the car they were traveling in sideswiped another car, hit a median and burst into flames Thursday night in the Gold Coast neighborhood. </p><p>A blue car was going south in the 1000 block of North DuSable Lake Shore Drive around 9:05 p.m. when it sideswiped a black car going in the same direction, Chicago police said. </p><p>The blue car then slammed into a median and burst into flames, leaving three people in the blue car injured. </p><p>A 21-year-old woman and two men, 22 and 20, were taken to Northwestern Memorial Hospital for treatment, police said. Their conditions were not given by police. </p><p>The driver of the black sedan, a 45-year-old man, declined medical attention, officials said. </p><p>No further information was available. </p>

entries.title: Membresías gratuitas de verano en los YMCAs atraen a 3,000 adolescentes de Chicago
entries.summary: <p>A Hailey Weathers le gusta pasar los veranos jugando voleibol en la arena con sus amigas en las playas de Chicago, tomando descansos entre partidos para bañarse en el Lago Michigan.</p><p>Pero a veces, la niña de 14 años siente que los adultos examinan todo lo que ella y sus amigas hacen, sobre todo cuando están en un grupo grande. Hailey sabe que eso se debe a que algunas concentraciones masivas de adolescentes se han vuelto problemáticas.</p><p>Pero ser observadas y juzgadas injustamente así la hace sentir incómoda, comentó.</p><p>“¿Por qué culpan a los adolescentes de cosas que no hacemos?”, cuestionó Hailey.</p><p>Por eso este verano Hailey también está tres días a la semana en la sede del South Side YMCA. Está en el gimnasio, en el laboratorio de computación o conversando con amigas.</p><p>Hailey es una de los miles de adolescentes que se registraron como miembros este verano a través del programa "Get Summer" del YMCA de la zona metropolitana de Chicago, una asociación con la Ciudad que ofrece membresías gratuitas a jóvenes de 12 a 18 años. Es la primera vez que Hailey es miembro.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-382e12" gratuita en el South Side YMCA para animarla a “salir de la casa”.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Casi 3,100 adolescentes se han inscrito en el programa desde junio en siete sedes de la ciudad, y la ubicación del lado sur recibió más de un tercio de las inscripciones. El YMCA no pudo decir cuántos eran miembros por primera vez, pero los responsables de las sedes participantes han notado un aumento en el flujo de gente y muchas caras nuevas.</p><p>Algunas ubicaciones con muchos recién llegados han tenido problemas de espacio, pero los funcionarios dijeron que es un buen problema. Las conversaciones sobre repetir el programa el próximo año están en marcha.</p><p>Hailey, que va a ingresar al noveno grado en Gary Comer College Prep, dijo que le encantaría volver.</p><p>“Deberían hacerlo el próximo verano porque me saca de la casa y puedo estar con gente en la que confío”, comentó.</p><p>Los funcionarios del YMCA esperaban que <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/03/ymca-free-summer-memberships-chicago-teens-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" >hasta 5,000 jóvenes</a> se registraran antes de que el programa terminara el 31 de agosto. Hasta el lunes, la organización había registrado 3,083 inscripciones en Get Summer.</p><p>Aunque probablemente no alcancen la meta original, “siendo esta la primera vez que lanzamos un programa así, lo consideramos extremadamente exitoso”, dijo un vocero del YMCA vía correo electrónico.</p><p>En el South Side YMCA se han inscrito 1,179 jóvenes, la mayor cantidad de las siete sedes que ofrecieron membresías gratuitas. El McCormick YMCA, en las áreas de Logan Square y Humboldt Park, registró 510 inscripciones, la segunda mayor cifra.</p><p>Los funcionarios anunciaron el programa de membresías gratuitas después de un fin de semana del Día de los Caídos empañado por los llamados “teen takeovers”, grandes concentraciones de jóvenes organizadas en redes sociales que a veces se han vuelto violentas.</p><p>Para frenar esas reuniones, algunos funcionarios locales han sugerido leyes de toque de queda más estrictas, más arrestos y multas para los padres cuyos hijos sean problemáticos. El alcalde Brandon Johnson y los funcionarios del YMCA respondieron que la mejor solución es ofrecer a los jóvenes más actividades gratuitas o asequibles y lugares seguros para reunirse.</p><p>La iniciativa de membresías gratuitas fue financiada enteramente con fondos filantrópicos, según dijo un portavoz de la oficina del alcalde. Mielle Cares, una fundación que aboga por el bienestar mental de los jóvenes, creó un fondo de $250,000 para ampliar las oportunidades de reunión centradas en la juventud en la ciudad, incluido el programa Get Summer.</p><p>Royce Holmes, de 15 años, dijo que no sabe cuál es el enfoque correcto para mantener seguras las grandes concentraciones de adolescentes, pero no cree que la solución sea restringir severamente a dónde pueden ir los jóvenes. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wsj.com/business/retail/teens-helped-bring-malls-back-to-life-now-theyre-getting-banned-37bdc2a9" target="_blank" >Cada vez más, los centros comerciales, las salas de cine</a> y otros negocios limitan cuándo los adolescentes pueden visitar sin un adulto acompañante.</p><p>“Siento que nos quita una gran parte de nuestra libertad”, agregó Royce. “Que nos prohíban estar en un lugar o que tengamos que irnos a cierta hora simplemente no suena bien”.</p><p>Royce, que va a ser estudiante de segundo año en Leo Catholic High School, también se inscribió para una membresía gratuita en el South Side YMCA este verano y además trabajó en esa sede durante unas semanas el año pasado a través de un programa de verano.</p><p>A menudo se le puede ver en la cancha de baloncesto, peleando por rebotes, repartiendo asistencias y practicando tiros. Ha notado más gente de su edad en la sede este verano. El aumento de miembros ha hecho que los partidos improvisados sean más competitivos y divertidos, dijo.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Royce Holmes, que empezará segundo año en Leo Catholic, dijo que el tiempo que ha podido pasar este verano en South Side YMCA gracias a su membresía gratuita lo ha ayudado a convertirse en mejor jugador de baloncesto.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Tyler Pasciak LaRiviere/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Kevin McGowan, quien fue director ejecutivo principal del South Side YMCA hasta principios de este mes, dijo que el gimnasio de baloncesto es uno de los espacios de reunión más populares para los nuevos miembros adolescentes. La piscina, el centro de fitness y el laboratorio de computación de la sede también están llenos.</p><p>McGowan dijo que las inscripciones en la sede del sur han superado las expectativas, pero no han alcanzado el tope de su capacidad. Para manejar el flujo, el personal controla los horarios de actividad e informa a los adolescentes cuándo los espacios están disponibles para ellos. Además, los jóvenes no llegan todos al mismo tiempo; van llegando a lo largo del día.</p><p>“Está lleno aquí, sin duda, pero realmente no hemos tenido problemas con demasiada gente en el edificio”, comentó McGowan. “Por supuesto, a la gente mayor no le gusta tener jóvenes cerca, pero se acostumbran”.</p><p>Él cree que la sede del sur ha recibido la mayoría de las nuevas inscripciones porque en la zona hay pocos lugares donde los muchachos tengan suficientes opciones para mantenerse ocupados y ser ellos mismos.</p><p>En el lado noroeste, la piscina del McCormick YMCA ha sido uno de los espacios más activos para los jóvenes este verano, según Mallory Munzel, quien supervisa la programación juvenil en los YMCAs de toda la ciudad.</p><p>Las nuevas multitudes allí han llevado al personal a ser prudente sobre cuánta gente puede entrar al gimnasio al mismo tiempo, pero no han tenido otros problemas de capacidad, dijo Munzel.</p><p>“Es emocionante ver a tantos adolescentes en el edificio todos los días”, añadió. “Me imagino que, por el nivel de participación, probablemente lo volveremos a hacer”.</p><p>Mientras muchos adolescentes vienen a jugar baloncesto, nadar o levantar pesas, algunos no tienen ganas de hacer nada en particular, dijo Munzel.</p><p>A menudo los programas centrados en jóvenes olvidan esto: a veces todo lo que un adolescente necesita es un espacio donde pueda no hacer nada, y no hay muchos lugares para eso, explicó. Los YMCAs de Chicago tienen sofás donde los adolescentes pueden relajarse y máquinas expendedoras con bocadillos en las áreas comunes. El South Side YMCA tiene un “salón para adolescentes” con videojuegos y una mesa de ping‑pong.</p><p>“Algunos solo quieren pasar el rato con sus amigos”, dijo Munzel. “Solo vienen a descansar”.</p><p>Royce y Hailey prefieren estar en grupos más pequeños. Se han topado con volantes en redes sociales para grandes reuniones en la playa o en el centro, pero dijeron que las evitan porque también han visto videos de las alteraciones que pueden estallar.</p><p>Ambos piensan contarles a amigos y familiares jóvenes sobre los programas del YMCA para que conozcan estas alternativas.</p><p>“Aquí es más fácil pasarla bien”, comentó Royce, “se siente más libre”.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Three positions to watch when Bears host Browns in preseason opener
entries.summary: <p>Three positions to watch Saturday when the Bears host the Browns at noon at Soldier Field:</p><h3>Left tackle</h3><p>With Braxton Jones out with a knee injury, the Bears will start Kiran Amegadjie and have him alternate quarters with Jedrick Wills.</p><p>Jones, when healthy, is the favorite to win the job. Saturday is a big opportunity for Wills, a former Browns first-round pick, and Amegadie to improve their status.</p><p>“There are too many things that are just not being done well enough,” offensive line coach Dan Roushar said.</p><h3>Wide receiver</h3><p>If the absence of Luther Burden and Zavion Thomas has made the receiver room slower, Ben Johnson hasn’t felt it. That’s a credit to UFL alum Kaden Davis, whom Johnson said “has made plays almost every single day,” and veteran Scotty Miller.</p><p>The two are competing for the Bears’ sixth wide receiver spot.</p><h3>Defensive tackle</h3><p>The Bears have tried to get rookie Jordan van den Berg, a sixth-round pick, to slow down in practice. His physicality, though, has earned him reps with the first team.</p><p>“I play with violence,” he said.</p><p>Saturday, for the first time, they’ll see how that translates to game action.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Empleado de limpieza muere días después de quedar atrapado en el fuego cruzado de un tiroteo en La Villita
entries.summary: <p>Se programó una autopsia para el viernes del empleado de limpieza que murió días después de que lo balearon mientras volvía a casa del trabajo a primera hora del sábado en el vecindario de La Villita.</p><p>Armando Viveros Cortés, de 35 años, formaba parte de un grupo de cuatro empleados que regresaban a casa en un vehículo a eso de las 2:40 a.m. el sábado en la cuadra 2400 al sur de Central Park Avenue, cuando se escucharon disparos y recibió un impacto en la cabeza, dijo la Policía de Chicago.</p><p>Los compañeros de trabajo de Viveros Cortés, que al principio creyeron que los estallidos eran fuegos artificiales, condujeron hasta la estación de policía del distrito de Ogden y tocaron la bocina hasta que los agentes salieron a ayudar, según un informe policial obtenido por el Sun-Times.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-4b0000" name="module-4b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La víctima, que iba como pasajero en el asiento trasero, fue trasladada al Hospital Mount Sinai, donde fue declarada muerta el miércoles a las 3:03 p.m., según la policía y la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook.</p><p>En la escena se encontraron al menos 27 casquillos, incluidos siete de 9 mm, según el informe policial.</p><p>Los detectives del Área 4 estaban investigando.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: White Sox put Davis Martin on injured list, call up Jose Urquidy
entries.summary: <p>DETROIT — The White Sox put right-hander Davis Martin on the 15-day injured list with a blister on his finger and sent Tanner McDougal back to Triple-A Charlotte on Friday. </p><p>They also called up righty José Urquidy and lefty Tyler Schweitzer from Charlotte. </p><p>Martin developed the blister on his middle finger Thursday during the Sox' 9-8 loss to the Reds. He blamed it and poor command for beaning the Reds' Sal Stewart, which got him ejected in the third inning. Stewart had homered in the first, and the umpires deemed Martin intended to hit him after throwing up and in before grazing the bill of his helmet. </p><p>Martin has been struggling for weeks, going 1-5 with a 7.06 ERA in his last 13 starts. The first inning has been a particular problem lately. In his last four starts, he has allowed 15 runs in the first.</p><p>The Sox acquired Urquidy, who will wear No. 70, on July 26 from the Pirates for righty Félix Doroteo. In three starts with Charlotte, Urquidy has a 2.25 ERA in 12 innings. Combined with the Pirates' Triple-A team in Indianapolis, he has a 3.48 ERA in 95 2/3 innings this season. Urquidy is in his seventh major-league season. His first five were with the Astros, for whom he pitched in the postseason each year. </p><p>He could see his first action tonight in the first of a three-game series against the second-place Tigers. Lefty Sean Newcomb will start a bullpen game for the first-place Sox, who could follow him with Urquidy. </p><p>McDougal, the Sox' seventh-ranked prospect, made his major-league debut Thursday and allowed one run on three walks and a hit batter in one-third of an inning. Schweitzer has a 2.78 ERA in 22 2/3 innings over four stints with the Sox this season, his first in the majors. He has one save and 11 strikeouts in 11 relief appearances. </p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" entries.title: Heather Mack’s ex-boyfriend asks to be released from jail ahead of trial in Bali murder conspiracy
entries.summary: <p>Following 12 years<b> </b>of incarceration<b> </b>over the sensational<b> </b>2014<b> </b>murder<b> </b>of Oak Park’s<b> </b>Sheila<b> </b>von<b> </b>Wiese-Mack<b> </b>in Indonesia,<b> </b>the man<b> </b>long<b> </b>accused<b> </b>of beating<b> </b>her<b> </b>to death<b> </b>is asking<b> </b>a federal judge<b> </b>in Chicago<b> </b>to let him out of jail.</p><p>Tommy<b> </b>Schaefer, 33,<b> </b>filed a motion for release<b> </b>Friday, moments before a scheduled appearance before<b> </b>U.S. District Judge<b> </b>Matthew<b> </b>Kennelly. The judge said he would consider the request during a hearing<b> </b>Aug. 27.</p><p>Schaefer made his request<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/heather-mack/2026/02/25/chicago-crime-heather-mack-tommy-schaefer-fbi-bali-indonesia" target="_blank" >six months after being returned</a> to Chicago<b> </b>from Indonesia, where he’d been imprisoned<b> </b>for<b> </b>more than 11 years over the 2014<b> </b>murder. He is the ex-boyfriend of Heather Mack, von Wiese-Mack’s daughter.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/heather-mack/2026/02/26/tommy-schaefer-wants-to-represent-himself-as-he-finally-faces-prosecution-for-murder-of-heather-macks-mom" >Tommy Schaefer wants to represent himself as he finally faces U.S. prosecution in death of Heather Mack’s mom</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Kennelly<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/17/24039349/heather-mack-gets-26-years-in-federal-prison-for-the-murder-of-her-mother-in-bali" target="_blank" >sentenced<b> </b>Mack</a>, 30, to<b> </b>26 years in prison<b> </b>in 2024 for conspiring<b> </b>with Schaefer<b> </b>to kill her<b> </b>mother<b> </b>overseas. Schaefer is set for trial<b> </b>Jan. 11.</p><p>Schaefer’s attorney, Michael<b> </b>Baker, argued in a four-page<b> </b>court filing<b> </b>Friday<b> </b>that Schaefer is not actually charged with a crime of violence<b> </b>in the United States. Rather, he is charged with conspiracy<b> </b>and<b> </b>obstruction of justice.</p><p>Baker went on to write that Schaefer<b> </b>suffers<b> </b>from<b> </b>“serious and ongoing health problems.” He<b> </b>contracted<b> </b>COVID-19<b> </b>in<b> </b>Indonesia, Baker wrote, and he’s since been diagnosed<b> </b>with a post-infectious condition. Cardiac evaluations<b> </b>are ongoing.</p><p>“The conditions of Mr. Schaefer’s pretrial detention are not adequate to properly monitor, manage, or treat his condition, and his continued incarceration delays the very evaluation his providers have ordered,” Baker wrote. “Release from custody, with conditions, would permit Mr. Schaefer to complete that workup and to obtain the medical care and monitoring his condition requires.”</p><p>Baker suggested electronic monitoring, home confinement and an unnamed<b> </b>third-party custodian. He denied<b> </b>that Schaefer<b> </b>is a flight risk<b> </b>or danger to the community.</p><p>Federal prosecutors are likely to oppose Schaefer’s request.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/17/24039349/heather-mack-gets-26-years-in-federal-prison-for-the-murder-of-her-mother-in-bali" >Heather Mack gets 26 years for murder of mom in Bali after stark testimony from family</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Mack and Schaefer are accused of planning von Wiese-Mack’s murder to access her $1.5 million estate. The killing triggered tabloid headlines around the world after her body was found stuffed in a suitcase outside the posh St. Regis Bali Resort.</p><p>Mack broached the idea of killing her mother with Schaefer as early as February 2014, the feds say. Schaefer wrote in a Facebook chat that month, “that b---- heather is crazy” and added “she asked me to find someone to kill her mom for 50k.”</p><p>The feds say Mack ultimately enlisted Schaefer, secretly booking a $12,000 plane ticket for him so he could rendezvous with her while she vacationed with her mother in Bali in August 2014.</p><p>Then, over the course of nearly 40 minutes on the morning of Aug. 12, 2014, prosecutors say Mack and Schaefer exchanged <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2015/9/24/18424089/heather-mack-traded-giddy-tense-texts-with-boyfriend-before-mom-s-murder" target="_blank" >tense, excited text messages</a> as they prepared to murder von Wiese-Mack. They allegedly used the phrase “saying hi” as code for the killing, and they referred to each other as Bonnie and Clyde.</p><p>Soon after, prosecutors say, von Wiese-Mack “was brutally beaten after being taken by surprise as she lay in her hotel bed.”</p><p>Mack’s<b> </b>plea agreement<b> </b>alleged that Schaefer<b> </b>“repeatedly beat [von Wiese-Mack] in the head and face,”<b> </b>ending her life.</p>

entries.title: No. 5 Nazareth reloads for 6A title run with a talented transfer QB and the dynamic Sakalas twins
entries.summary: <p>Hank and Henry Sakalas have piles of memories from the countless hours they’ve spent playing football together. The Nazareth twins are full of appreciation for those special moments. But they are brothers, and even the closest siblings will get on each other’s nerves.</p><p>“In meetings [Henry] is always talking, always trying to coach everyone up,” Hank Sakalas said. “He’s always talking and sometimes it is frustrating. But I love playing with him. I wouldn’t change it for the world.”</p><p>College football careers are long, unpredictable and often contain many stops. So no one knows what the future holds. But for now, the twins assume this is the last season they will play football together.</p><p>“We grew up playing together, and it is tough now knowing that is coming to an end,” Henry Sakalas said. “So this season is bittersweet. But we have all these memories and it has been truly special.”</p><p>Henry is a 6-3, 195-pound safety committed to Michigan State. Hank is 6-2, 220 pounds and is heading to D2 Southwest Minnesota State. He played all over the field last season, putting in time at linebacker, tight end and wide receiver.</p><p>“The dinner table at home is all Nazareth football right now,” Hank Sakalas said. “It is really exciting to get this last ride with my brother.”</p><p>A mountain of college-bound football talent surrounds the Sakalas twins, and the No. 5 Roadrunners have the perfect coach in place to take advantage. Tim Racki has won 10 state titles in his career and produced three NFL players (Julian Love, JJ McCarthy, Tanner Koziol).</p><p>“The [Sakalas family] is amazing,” Racki said. “They are great kids and great leaders. They are smart in the classroom, everyone loves them in the school, and they bring it on the field, too.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> entries.title: Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to federal stalking charges in the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK (AP) — <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/unitedhealthcare-ceo-brian-thompson-shooting-luigi-mangione-10ee2f70cd843a27940a9cf1a06edf55" target="_blank" >Luigi Mangione</a> pleaded guilty on Friday to federal stalking charges in the 2024 killing of <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/united-healthcare-ceo-new-york-shooting-brian-thompson-8a130e64bcab749d1a085f5a34ab8254" target="_blank" >UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson</a>.</p><p>Mangione, 28, entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death. With this guilty plea, his lawyers could seek to have the state case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.</p><p>Mangione was charged by both federal and state prosecutors with <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/manhattan-shooting-death-daa1e8c8c05606197a5bd2e0242f1683" target="_blank" >ambushing Thompson</a>, 50, outside a New York City hotel on Dec. 4, 2024, as the insurance executive walked to his company’s annual investor conference.</p><p>Surveillance video of the killing showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson from behind. Police say “delay,” “deny” and “depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims. That detail — and revelations that Mangione’s private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities — made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/united-healthcare-ceo-luigi-mangione-josh-shapiro-3a8c64a0bc412e0eeb84bca0c99b6e67" target="_blank" >cause célèbre</a> for some of its critics.</p><p>Mangione <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/luigi-mangione-united-healthcare-ceo-d148fbdde498c3ea4cf768945889d7e7" target="_blank" >never was a UnitedHealthcare customer</a>, according to police and the company. A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/unitedhealthcare-ceo-shooting-suspect-c68d0328f278d85fcf201ae89f634098" target="_blank" >was arrested five days after the shooting</a>, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Altoona, Pennsylvania. It’s about 230 miles west of Manhattan.</p><p>Thompson led one of the United States’ largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry. Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021.</p><p>A trial on state murder charges is scheduled to start next month. It is unclear whether that trial would go forward if Mangione pleaded guilty in the federal case.</p><p>The federal charges accuse Mangione of stalking Thompson to cause his death. Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed Mangione to a potential death penalty.</p><p>Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any common sense definition.”</p><p>Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.</p><p>The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.</p><p>In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.</p><p>U.S. District Judge Margaret M. Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defense, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.</p><p>They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/mangione-united-health-care-ceo-killed-3f6326b0a8fdf807622746a5d461742c" target="_blank" >a notebook</a> in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.</p><p>In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defense in the state case but <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/luigi-mangione-psychiatric-defense-unitedhealthcare-killing-aeada6e00f25153c5860643f27e6b299" target="_blank" >reversed course</a> a day later. The defense, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.</p>

entries.title: As the Chicago mayoral race gets underway, what issue is most important? Here's what you told us
entries.summary: <p>With the Chicago mayoral race starting, we asked readers what issue is most important. Here's what you told us, lightly edited for clarity:</p><p>“Housing — increasing the supply despite neighbors’ objections. Eliminating aldermanic privilege.”<br><i>— Kelly Kleiman</i></p><p>“I'm mainly concerned about property tax relief for seniors; we've paid our share for decades now.”<br><i>— Christine Bock</i></p><p>“The most important thing to me is finding the root cause of things. Be proactive, not reactive. Example: the CTA figured out people jumping the turnstile led to more crime, so they have started to fix that.”<br><i>— Dean R. Martin</i></p><p>"Housing prices, transit, electric scooters on the sidewalks."</p><p><i>— Lori Miller Barrett</i></p><p></p><p>“Developing a structure that is sustainable pertaining to public employees' pension plans. Kicking the problem down the road has created a massive burden on taxpayers.”<br><i>— P. Teodo</i></p><p>"The continued infrastructure investments on the South and West sides of Chicago. The West Side, in particular, has been disinvested in for years."<br><i>— Larry Williamson</i></p><p>"Public safety comes first. We need leadership that backs law enforcement, protects law-abiding citizens and spends taxpayer dollars responsibly. That’s why I’ll be voting for the most conservative candidate."<br><i>— Brian Allen</i></p><p>"Improving mass transit, cycling infrastructure, walkability."<br><i>— Jean Pabon</i></p><p>"I’m tired of the culture war BS and would prefer local government continue to focus on real issues such as public safety, taxes, and supporting small businesses. The Hispanic communities will need extra support as the ICE debacle has crippled local businesses in some neighborhoods."<br><i>— Ernest Krolick</i></p><p>"Underfunded pension liabilities, transportation, infrastructure, housing and paying for it all."<br><i>— Carlos Javier Ochoa Andrade</i></p><p>"Cost of living: rent is too high, food costs too much, and seniors are having a hard time aging in place."<br><i>— Gerald Farinas</i></p><p>"No more hiring cops. entries.title: Chicago murals: Stacey King tribute in Logan Square was passion project for artist Darius Dennis
entries.summary: <p>Artist Darius Dennis grew up watching the Chicago Bulls championship dynasty in the 1990s. Stacey King played on the first three of those teams to win titles.</p><p>Dennis had King’s autographed rookie card after the Bulls picked the former University of Oklahoma star in the first round of the 1989 NBA draft. Years after the 1990s dynasty, Dennis regularly listened to King after he returned and spent two more decades providing color commentary for Bulls games. Dennis remembers turning his television from the national broadcasts to the local stations, just to hear King.</p><p>So <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/06/07/bulls-announce-former-broadcaster-player-stacey-king-died" >when King died in June at age 59</a>, Dennis says, he knew he had to do something to
