class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Darius Dennis stands in front of the mural he painted of Stacey King.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jim Vondruska/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“If no one steps up to the plate and paints a Stacey King portrait before I’m free, I’ve got to do it,” Dennis recalls thinking.</p><p>So Dennis, a Chicago native who works full time as owner and artist with Big Wall Sign and Mural, painted it himself. His 17-foot-tall, detailed portrait of King, complete with an outline of the Chicago Bull mascot wearing a graffiti-style crown, is at Project Logan, a rotating graffiti permission wall behind 2929 W. Fullerton Avenue in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/logan-square" >Logan Square</a>.</p><p>The mural also includes one of King's catchphrases, “Too big, too strong, too fast, too good!”</p><p>Dennis painted the mural, he says, because in Chicago’s graffiti culture it’s important to do rest-in-peace tribute murals. Artists in coastal cities do it more than those in Chicago, Dennis says.</p><p>“Stacey King is the Harry Caray of our generation,” says Dennis, comparing King to the late Cubs’ legendary announcer. “He deserves to be painted and remembered.”</p><p>Others seem to agree. One weekday morning a Chicago Police car paused by the mural before driving on. And a man stopped and snapped photos, including selfies, in front of King’s image before he, too, went on his way.</p><p>“Stacey is getting his Bigsby & Kruthers today,” Dennis says, referring to the portraits of Michael Jordan and Dennis Rodman in the 1990s, when the Chicago menswear company added hand-painted images of the Bulls stars on its warehouse along the Kennedy Expressway. The murals reportedly caused traffic jams and had to be removed amid safety concerns.</p><p>Another mural by Dennis also went viral this summer. His <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals/2026/07/24/chicago-murals-john-prine-lincoln-square-darius-dennis-jon-langford" >portrait of folk music legend John Prine</a> at Old Town School of Folk Music in Lincoln Square took off on social media.</p><p>“I didn’t expect it to get this crazy this quick,” Dennis says. “I’ve been scratching my head. Oh, I did that.”</p><p>While the Prine mural was commissioned, the King mural is one Dennis took on by himself. He picked the Project Logan wall because he respected it as a traditional Chicago graffiti permission wall, and he knows the person who runs it. Also, he loved Stacey King.</p><p>“I need one to two projects a year that are just for me and I can paint from the heart,” he says. This mural was that project.</p><p>“I watched all the championship games as a kid. I’m Bulls forever.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2026/06/07/bulls-announce-former-broadcaster-player-stacey-king-died" >Former Bulls player and broadcaster Stacey King dies at 59</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals/2026/07/24/chicago-murals-john-prine-lincoln-square-darius-dennis-jon-langford" >John Prine mural adorns Old Town School of Folk Music</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics/2024/11/15/chicago-murals-darius-dennis-cta-red-line-civil-rights-danny-lyon-toddle-house-uptown" >Civil Rights Movement sit-in photo in Uptown is the subject of Darius Dennis’ Red Line mural</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d00000" name="module-d00000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Murals and Mosaics Newsletter</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-990000" name="html-embed-module-990000"></a><div class="piano-sidebar-newsletter-murals-and-mosaics"></div> </div> </div></div> </div><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-b20000" name="module-b20000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Chicago’s murals and mosaics sidebar</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/murals-mosaics" target="_blank" >Chicago’s murals & mosaics</a></h3>Part of a series on public art in the city and suburbs. <b>Know of a mural or mosaic? entries.title: 4 artsy spots to visit in Chicago’s Austin neighborhood
entries.summary: <p>Chicago’s Austin neighborhood is experiencing a resurgence, spurred by the development of new businesses, mixed-income housing and health and workforce centers along Chicago Avenue. </p><p>After a section of the thoroughfare was christened “Soul City Corridor,” the state designated the community as the<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/arts-and-culture/2026/08/14/chicago-austin-neighborhood-arch-public-art-soul-city-illinois-cultural-district" > “Soul City” cultural district. </a>The moniker celebrates the area's potential to grow into a thriving arts scene. Here are just four of the organizations working toward that effort.</p><h2>The Kehrein Center for the Arts</h2><p>Owned by the Catalyst Circle Rock Charter School, the venue has hosted community events and a diverse lineup of performances, from Chicago Jazz Philharmonic concerts to theatrical productions about West Side activists. The restored mid-century modern auditorium is also the official home of the El Sistema Ravinia student orchestra, comprising musicians from Chicago Public Schools. </p><p>The goal of the center is to be a meeting place for the community, provide a platform for artists and contribute to the overall development of Austin, said Ed Siderewicz, co-founder of Catalyst Circle Rock Charter School. <i>5628 W. Through its “redemptive plastics” program, the organization repurposes materials into art, furniture and tools. entries.title: NFL commissioner met with Illinois lawmakers Thursday: report
entries.summary: <p>On the same day that <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> president/CEO Kevin Warren and chairman George McCaskey claimed they’d had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/08/13/bears-stadium-update-hammond-arlington-heights-george-mccaskey-kevin-warren-chairman-president-indiana-illinois-nfl" target="_blank" >“minimal” conversations</a> recently with local lawmakers about a stadium funding plan, NFL commissioner Roger Goodell reportedly met with Illinois officials Thursday.</p><p>Politico reported Friday morning that he met with a “few select Illinois lawmakers” Thursday. The commissioner’s office declined comment.</p><p>It’s unlikely the commissioner would hold any sort of meeting, informal or not, without the Bears’ blessing. The team has continued to declare Hammond, Indiana, as the sole focus of its stadium site search — but the Bears still haven't closed the door to staying in Illinois. That has kept at least slim hopes alive for them to try to work out a funding plan with local politicians, who are out of the legislative session.</p><p>Thursday, McCaskey made it sound like the NFL’s stadium committee, of which he’s a member, might need some convincing to allow the move across state lines.</p><p>“We think that, ultimately, they will become comfortable,” he said.</p><p>The Bears, meanwhile, are continuing their stadium slog, one that started more than five years ago and has yanked fans’ hopes around like a tug-of-war rope. The Bears have alternately declared sites on the Lakefront, in Arlington Heights and in Hammond, Ind., as their preferred site for a fixed-roof domed stadium. The Hammond plan is the only one that reached, and passed, a vote of the Bears’ vote of directors to move forward. When the Bears announced in June that their focus was shifting to Indiana, team officials told Illinois political leaders that they looked forward to continuing to work with them.</p><p>The Bears own 326 acres in Arlington Heights. They've pledged to put $2 billion toward a stadium in Hammond, where one site has been declared viable and the other is undergoing environmental and topographical testing. </p><p>Goodell, whose wife Jane went to Lake Forest High School and was raised a Bears fan, has toured sites in Hammond and Arlington Heights. He <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/03/31/nfl-commissioner-roger-goodell-bears-need-stadium-solution-soon-arlington-heights-hammond-indiana-annual-meetings" entries.title: Violence prevention founder, CPS employee charged with sexually assaulting and grooming girls
entries.summary: <p>The founder of a violence prevention program on Chicago’s South Side has been accused of sexually assaulting and grooming two teenage girls over the course of more than seven years.</p><p>Charles McKenzie, 37, was charged with the two felony counts on Aug. 7 and was ordered held at the Cook County Jail, court records show.</p><p>McKenzie founded Englewood First Responders, a nonprofit focused on violence prevention that has <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicago.gov/city/en/sites/community-safety/home/PeoplesPlanforCommunitySafety/cvi-program.html" target="_blank" ><u>partnered with the city</u></a> and has earned <a class="Link" href="https://illinoiscomptroller.gov/financial-reports-data/find-a-report/state-contracts" target="_blank" ><u>lucrative contracts</u></a> from the state. He also has worked as a counseling assistant at Chicago Public Schools and was still employed by the district when he was arrested earlier this month, according to court records.</p><p>The allegations stretch back to September 2019, when McKenzie is accused of sexually assaulting a girl who was as young as 14 at the time, according to Cook County prosecutors.</p><p>McKenzie allegedly made “sexual facial gestures” toward the girl and grabbed her inappropriately while she was playing at a youth center where he worked.</p><p>The girl told her sister and eventually her mother, but police weren’t immediately notified, prosecutors said.</p><p>The girl then set up a FaceTime call with McKenzie so her sister could see how he behaved, prosecutors said. After allegedly asking the girl to show him the room to make sure she was alone, he exposed himself to her and made more explicit facial gestures.</p><p>The girl’s sister took screenshots but their mother “did nothing” to alert the authorities, court records show.</p><p>McKenzie sexually abused that girl’s relative in March 2026 while she was laying in bed, prosecutors said. The 14-year-old girl tried to stop him, but the attack allegedly continued until McKenzie ultimately relented.</p><p>The girl told her mother, who said she’d “handle it,” but officials weren’t alerted, prosecutors said. The girl then told the first alleged victim, who called police.</p><p>McKenzie made "general denials" in response to the allegations but identified himself and the first girl in a screenshot. He alternated between claiming the photo was fake and saying it was from an old call, prosecutors said.</p><p>His attorney didn’t respond to a request for comment, and his organization could not be reached.</p><p>In a statement, CPS said it “prioritizes and takes seriously its responsibility to ensure the safety, security, and well-being of all students,” but that it does not comment on ongoing investigations.</p><p>Launched in 2019, Englewood First Responders has held community events, offered mentoring and after-school programming and conducted daily walk-throughs of the neighborhood. In 2024, Green told the Sun-Times about the burden of mitigating violent incidents.</p><p>“I don’t get sleep because I’m trying to keep a lot of stuff down in the community,” he said.</p><p>He’s expected back in court Aug. 26.</p>

entries.title: Chicago area under flood watch Friday night through Saturday morning
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago area could see more flooding as heavy rainfall is expected Friday night into Saturday morning, according to the National Weather Service.</p><p>A flood watch is in effect for much of the Chicago area, especially south of Interstate 80, from 10 p.m. Friday through 10 a.m. Saturday, according to the weather service. Water from creeks and streams could rise out of their banks and urban areas with poor drainage could also flood in Chicago and suburbs as far as Naperville and Calumet City.</p><p>The flood watch comes as the Chicago area has seen some of the most severe storms in recent memory this summer, which have caused damage to homes, widespread flooding and, for the first time, nearly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/06/chicago-deep-tunnel-historic-flooding-tarp-reservoir-weather-climate-change" >filled the reservoirs</a> meant to manage storm water and flooding. The effects of storms can be cumulative, and flooding can happen even with small amounts of rain if the ground has already had to handle a lot of water, according to NWS meteorologist Brett Borchardt.</p><p>"That's what's setting the table for the potential flash floods tonight," Borchardt said. "The ground is really saturated and can't really take much water.</p><p>Central Illinois is likely to see the worst of the storm impacts because the area got heavy rain Thursday night, Borchardt said. Chicago and the northern suburbs are still likely to see rain and storms, but the further south you get, the more rain and flooding are possible, he said. </p><p>"The threat for rain is higher down there. [I] wouldn't be surprised if folks wake up to some rumbles of thunder as early as 3, 4 in the morning," he said.</p><p>A flood watch was issued for the area <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/09/heavy-rain-flash-flooding-possible-in-chicago-area-overnight" >earlier this week</a>. Residents in the south suburbs and northwest Indiana are still <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/13/northwest-indiana-tornadoes-clean-up" >grappling with the effects of tornadoes and other severe storms</a> from earlier in the summer. </p>

entries.title: Reportan la doceava muerte relacionada con el calor y las temperaturas de verano en el Condado de Cook
entries.summary: <p>Según la Oficina del Médico Forense del Condado de Cook, una doceava persona ha muerto por causas relacionadas con el calor vinculadas a las temperaturas extremas de este verano.</p><p>Jesús Rodríguez, de 33 años, murió el 17 de julio por hipertermia y exposición al calor ambiental, además de toxicidad por cocaína, según la oficina del forense. Es el más joven de la docena de muertes relacionadas con el calor este año.</p><p>El Condado de Cook ha registrado más muertes relacionadas con el calor en 2026 que en cualquier otro año de la última década, según un <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/07/30/extreme-heat-wave-death-chicago-cook-county-oak-lawn-july-stroke-stress-elderly-air-conditioning" target="_blank" >análisis de WBEZ y Chicago Sun-Times</a> de los datos del forense. Nueve de los 12 eran residentes de Chicago y casi todos vivían en el lado sur.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-f50000" name="module-f50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Todas menos una ocurrieron en julio. La primera muerte relacionada con el calor de este año se registró el 1 de julio.</p><p>El condado ha visto otros años con varias muertes relacionadas con el calor. El Condado de Cook registró seis muertes en 2019 y otras seis en 2022.</p><p>La siguiente muerte por calor más reciente ocurrió el martes, cuando Otto Kedzior falleció por complicaciones de una enfermedad cardiovascular y <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/weather/2026/08/05/cook-county-10th-heat-related-death-2026" target="_blank" >estrés por calor</a> en la cuadra 1000 al sur de Wood Street, dijeron las autoridades. Tenía 64 años.</p><p>Pero la mayoría de las muertes ocurrieron durante las varias olas de calor extremo de julio.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-870000" name="html-embed-module-870000"></a><div style="min-height:531px" id="datawrapper-vis-WIr6T"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WIr6T/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-WIr6T"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/WIr6T/full.png" alt="Twelve people have died so far this year in Cook County from heat-related causes, the most in at least a decade (Column Chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Claramont Little, del vecindario de Greater Grand Crossing, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/health/2026/08/12/heat-stroke-record-death-chicago-cook-county-medical-examiner-office-stress-elderly-senior" target="_blank" >murió en la madrugada del 2 de julio</a> en la misma cuadra donde vivía, dijeron las autoridades. El forense determinó recientemente que su muerte fue causada por un golpe de calor.</p><p>Otros cuyas muertes se han atribuido al menos en parte al calor este año incluyen a Joseph Huff, de 65 años; Robert Feldon, de 77; Stephanie Rodríguez, de 45; David González, de 44; Barbara Whigham, de 71; Mike Rodríguez, de 57; Daniel Machnikowski, de 69; Victor Ferguson, de 48; y David P. Sopys, de 46.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>

entries.title: Cubs' Edward Cabrera will return to rotation on Sunday vs. Cardinals
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> right-hander Edward Cabrera, on the injured list since June 24 with a left hamstring/adductor strain, is expected to rejoin the rotation and start on Sunday in the finale of the series against the St. Louis Cardinals.</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell made the announcement before Friday’s game, after Cabrera threw a bullpen season. Left-hander Shota Imanaga, who had been slated to start on Sunday against the Cardinals' Hunter Dobbins, will pitch Monday's opener of a three-game set against the White Sox at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Cabera is 5-4 with a 5.10 ERA over 14 games, all starts, in his first season with the Cubs.</p><p>Cabrera was hurt when he stretched for a throw at first base on June 23 during a 9-6 win over the Mets in New York. He did splits on the play, came up limping and had to be carted off the field.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">The cart is out for Cubs pitcher Edward Cabrera after he suffered an apparent injury covering first base to end the fifth inning <a href="https://t.co/1ppBBAe5fX">pic.twitter.com/1ppBBAe5fX</a></p>— SNY (@SNYtv) <a href="https://x.com/SNYtv/status/2069591357555937506?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 24, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>In May and June, the 28-year-old Cabrera missed two weeks with a blister on his right middle finger.</p><p>Counsell didn’t specify restrictions for Cabrera in his return, but said “I think normal first start off the injured list caution.”</p><p>Cabrera was acquired from Miami in the offseason in a trade that sent prospects Owen Caissie, Cristian Hernandez and Edgardo De Leon to the Marlins.</p><p>Counsell said he wasn’t sure who might be shifted from the Cubs rotation after Cabrera’s return. He didn’t envision the Cubs going to a six-man rotation at this time.</p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: This year's version of the Cubs is much more believable as a contender
entries.summary: <p><i>“No one performs an experiment once and considers the work done. They repeat it with different variables, correcting what they thought they knew, adding what they’ve learned.” </i></p><p>— from “The School of Life” by Amy Maclin as it appeared in O Daily Magazine</p><p>At some point this season — maybe it was during their first 10-game winning streak in late April, maybe it was during their second, maybe at some point during the 10-game losing streak that followed in late May, maybe they’re in the midst of it right now during their 8-2 run since the Dodgers series in which they’ve been playing some of their best and most meaningful baseball all season — the Cubs fell into a sense of belief in themselves.</p><p>As if they had found, to some unexpected degree, a deeper purpose.</p><p>We’ll never know. They’ll never outwardly say. At least not until they win it all or once it ends. That’s the way it should be.</p><p>Belief can be a thing of beauty or betrayal. Last season, the Cubs believed. Maybe not hard enough, maybe not real enough, but either one of two things happened: Their belief in self betrayed them or the truth did what the truth does.</p><p>This season, at the 75%-of-the-season-done threshold, their belief, we can all believe, is different. Rooted in something more real. Rooted in a greater sense of self-truth.</p><p>One through nine, no matter where manager Craig Counsell wants to put them in the lineup, these Cubs can put up numbers and men on base as fast as any team — if not faster than any team — in all of baseball. Against just about anyone any team puts on the mound. Sweeping the Dodgers in that three-game series is so not the same as being locked into seeing the Dodgers over seven games in September or October. But it’s the consistency of showing out after that series that speaks the loudest. Carries the most lasting meaning.</p><p>Damn the latest Dansby Swanson slump (7-for-38 since the Cardinals series in July before a breakout game against the Nationals on Wednesday, which included a 436-foot “see ya” in the seventh inning, somewhat confirming the “He’s made the adjustments” stamp by hitting coach Dustin Kelly). Damn Alex Bregman’s first-half low-show. Now he’s playing like he’s jealous of Pete Crow-Armstrong’s National League MVP position and conversations. He switched to using Swanson’s bat July 27 and is hitting .388 with six home runs since.</p><p>This is where they are. Most feared offensively, most respected defensively. Pitching — starting, middle relief, closers — still far from defined. But more important than what we’re supposed to make of them, where are the Cubs with themselves?</p><p>It feels good to the outside world of Cubdom to watch them put up 20 runs in the first two games of a series against the Nationals, but what should that same world do with the one-hit shutout the Nats put on them to end that series?</p><p>Those 10-game extremes of April and May, of clustered and stacked losses and wins, won’t disappear. They remain the difference in a team being “streaky” and a team that carries that tag of being “volatile” in performance.</p><p>Still, this is what Joe, Tom, Todd, Laura and Pete (Ricketts) wanted from an ownership perspective. A team that was in search of self while winning at the same time. A team finding a path greater than just wining the NL Central. A team that makes an $845 million purchase 17 years ago, now valued at north of $5 billion, seem worth twice as much. The MLB Lakers in a certain context. Hot. The “it” franchise regardless of championships. The best of all baseball worlds.</p><p>But this team internally seems to be beyond all of that. So the Cubs sit. One of four teams (Arizona, San Diego, Philadelphia) battling for top position in the NL wild-card race, with a 6œ-game lead over the closest wannabe, with seven games left against the Brewers to close the three-game gap Milwaukee has on them for the division crown.</p><p>Pressing neither the panic nor patience button.</p><p>Psychology Today tells us beliefs are not absolute truths. They are tools that exist on a spectrum between fact and faith. Facts are objective realities that remain true whether we believe in them or not. Faith is absolute conviction without evidence, a leap beyond what the senses or science can verify.</p><p>Maybe the Cubs’ belief, to get past their own past coming back to haunt them, is (with all due respect to last postseason, hitting .200 as a team in the NL Division Series): All nine bats can’t go cold at the same time. Not this time. But just what are they to do during the last quarter of the season while fighting the demons unsubstantiated belief can have on a team?</p><p>For the experiment that has been the Cubs’ season, belief is the only habit that breeds confidence. So if they lead by faith, the bats will follow.<br></p>

entries.title: Pritzker signs bill to provide damage relief to homeowners ravaged by flooding
entries.summary: <p>Illinois homeowners impacted by flood damage from powerful storms that hit the state will have help with recovery through a new program signed into law by Gov. JB Pritzker.</p><p>Severe storms and flooding damage across the state have prompted lawmakers to make relief efforts more accessible, according to the governor’s office.</p><p>Following the signing of Senate Bill 3925 into law on Friday, homeowners in the state will be able to participate in disaster relief programs that are typically not covered under standard insurance policies.</p><p>“Last summer, severe storms and flooding hit communities across Illinois – leaving hardworking families with thousands in unexpected costs,” Pritzker said in a news release from his office. With the new law, “we are giving communities another tool to help homeowners recover. When Washington refuses to help, we will keep fighting for you while we find ways to help each other.”</p><p>Under the new law, the Southwest Equity Home Assurance Program and the Northwest Home Equity Assurance Program can establish legislation that builds on the Home Equity Assurance Act. </p><p>A temporary, three-year flood damage direct rebate program will be available to homeowners, and eligible households will get a one-time rebate for up to 50% of flood-related expenses, with a maximum rebate of $1,000, according to the release.</p><p>These relief programs come as the federal government declines to help with natural disaster recovery, the governor’s office said in the release. </p><p>Two storms in 2025 brought <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2025/08/26/city-issues-disaster-proclamation-for-areas-affected-by-rain-flooding" >heavy rainfall and flash flooding</a> to parts of the south, southwest and west sides of Chicago, but the Trump administration failed to provide FEMA assistance, the release said. </p><p>At the time, Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/02/09/trump-administration-denial-illinois-appeal-summer-storms-disaster-relief?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=02102026%20Morning%20Edition&utm_content=02102026%20Morning%20Edition+CID_68c0311a3381c920948e67a69042a1e8&utm_source=cst_campaign_monitor&utm_term=Illinois%20appeal%20for%20summer%20storm%20disaster%20relief%20is%20denied%20by%20Trump%20administration&tpcc=cst_cm" target="_blank" >said the denials</a> were politically motivated, because the president approved similar assistance to other states, like North Dakota and Alaska.</p><p>“At the end of the day, this is about the same thing we've always been about: maintaining homeownership and stabilizing our neighborhoods,” Victoria Gaspar, executive director of the Southwest Home Equity Assurance Program, said in the release. “Flooding can be one of the most disruptive and costly things a homeowner faces, and this bill gives us a real tool to help our members recover and stay put. Programs like this, household by household, are what keep our neighborhoods strong.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/04/10/flooding-chicago-climate-change-deep-tunnel-mold-metropolitan-water-reclamation-district-soaked" >Flooding in Chicago is getting worse. Here’s why.</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Trump’s America keeps getting worse
entries.summary: <p>In October 1980, then-candidate Ronald Reagan asked voters a very important question: “Are you better off than you were four years ago?”</p><p>It was during the only televised debate he had against incumbent President Jimmy Carter, whose presidency had been marred by one crisis after another, from record-high inflation and rising unemployment, to soaring gas prices and the Iran hostage crisis.</p><p>Reagan knew the answer to his question was a resounding “no,” and asking it helped propel him to a landslide victory. It also became a regularly invoked rhetorical feature of presidential campaigns going forward.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-380000" name="module-380000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnists bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2><br><i>In-depth political coverage, sports analysis, entertainment reviews and cultural commentary.</i><br></div> </div><p>No one knows the cautionary tale of Carter’s presidency more than our current president, who has repeatedly used it as a stand-in for presidential failure and American weakness. Although Carter’s legacy greatly improved in the years since leaving office, he ended his only term with a bleak 34% approval rating.</p><p>Donald Trump's approval rating currently sits at an abysmal 32%, <a class="Link" href="https://www.app.com/story/news/2026/08/13/trump-approval-rating-aug-13-2026/91283891007/" target="_blank" >according to Quinnipiac’s latest polling</a>, and likely for many of the same reasons Carter finished where he did, ironically — high inflation, rising gas prices and a foreign policy crisis in Iran.</p><p>So, <a class="Link" href="https://today.marquette.edu/2026/08/new-marquette-law-school-poll-national-survey-finds-inflation-and-cost-of-living-the-most-important-issue-economy-next-most-important/" target="_blank" >the question</a> of whether voters are better off than they were two years ago isn’t hard to answer for most — in January of this year just 28% said they were better off than they were a year ago, and in July that number had dropped to 19%.</p><p>And it’s no wonder — when you move beyond the economic numbers, which are bad enough, the picture of Trump’s America gets worse with every peek behind the MAGA curtain.</p><p>In fact, it can feel at times like America has become a Third World country.</p><p>Case in point, the U.S. is in the midst of a measles outbreak, with more cases than it’s seen in more than three decades, thanks to the administration’s vaccine misinformation. We are now at risk of losing our official <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/measles-outbreak-us-map-2026/" target="_blank" >measles elimination status</a>, which we’ve held for more than a quarter-century.</p><p>We’re also facing no fewer than 11 foodborne illness outbreaks, including two separate cyclospora outbreaks, as well as <a class="Link" href="https://www.foodandwine.com/fda-foodborne-outbreak-investigations-12034027" target="_blank" >outbreaks</a> of listeria, salmonella and E. coli, all since Trump downsized oversight agencies, dropped food facility inspections and stripped back mandatory reporting requirements at the federal Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network.</p><p>Trump’s dumb war in Iran has <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us-has-used-virtually-all-its-long-range-precision-missiles-during-iran-war-2026-08-04/" target="_blank" >depleted</a> American munitions significantly — up to 80% in some categories — straining stockpiles and raising readiness concerns. And there are new <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediaite.com/media/news/sailors-on-uss-abraham-lincoln-reportedly-take-desperate-measures-amid-months-long-deployment-and-poor-conditions/" target="_blank" >reports</a> of sailors on the USS Abraham Lincoln, deployed to the North Arabian Sea since November, desperately jumping overboard amid poor conditions — from clogged toilets to mildewed showers, food supply problems to mental health concerns.</p><p>This is America — the superpower? Where college grads can’t find work, where housing is <a class="Link" href="https://www.bankrate.com/mortgages/american-dream-of-homeownership-turning-into-luxury/" target="_blank" >unaffordable for 75%</a> of the population, where families must choose between paying rent or paying doctors bills? Where you can be shot dead for peacefully protesting? Where your government is shuttering important health agencies while spewing junk science about autism and Tylenol? Where our allies are skeptical of us, and our enemies no longer seem to fear us?</p><p>While Trump fiddles with reflecting pools, golden statues and ballrooms, it feels like America is burning, becoming less and less formidable and functional with every passing day.</p><p>And Republicans are asking for two more years of control of it all. Who could possibly want more of this?</p><p>Upon the occasion of Carter’s 100th birthday in October 2024, Trump did what Trump does — and insulted him. But only to insult former President Joe Biden worse, saying Carter was happy because he “is considered a brilliant president by comparison.”</p><p>Just think what they’ll say about Trump — overseeing all of this chaos, destruction, corruption and incompetence.</p><p>“Are you better off?” Are you kidding?</p><p><i>S.E. Cupp is the host of “S.E. Cupp Unfiltered” on CNN.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-010000" name="module-010000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Cubs starter Clay Holmes shuts down Cardinals in 3-0 victory
entries.summary: <p>Cubs newcomer Clay Holmes and his sinker were back in form. </p><p>Sensational form.</p><p>Holmes was dominant in his second start and home debut with the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" target="_blank" >Cubs</a>, tossing one-hit ball into the seventh inning and leading the North Siders past the St. Louis Cardinals 3-0 on Friday afternoon at Wrigley Field.</p><p>Seiya Suzuki hit his 21<sup>st </sup>homer, a three-run shot in the sixth, to break a scoreless tie and added a double in the eighth for his fourth two-hit game in his last six. The Cubs kept the pressure on National League Central-leading Milwaukee with their ninth win in 11.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="in" dir="ltr">Seiya later! <br><br>Seiya Suzuki gives the <a href="https://x.com/Cubs?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">@Cubs</a> the lead 💪 <a href="https://t.co/aIFWLngK92">pic.twitter.com/aIFWLngK92</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2088355085298327910?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">August 14, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>Less than 24 hours after getting one-hit in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/13/after-two-big-nights-showed-bats-potential-cubs-nearly-no-hit-in-battle-of-baseballs-top-offenses" target="_blank" >7-0 loss in Washington</a>, the Cubs turned the tables by shutting down their next opponent.</p><p>Holmes walked just one in 6⅔ innings and bounced back impressively from a rocky first outing with the Cubs, last Saturday at Kansas City, after they had acquired him from the New York Mets at the trade deadline. The 33-year-old right-hander allowed four runs on six hits in four innings in a 6-3 loss to the Royals as he came back off the 60-day injured list and started a big league game for the first time since May 15.</p><p>Against the Cards, Holmes was dealing from the get-go, retiring the first 16 hitters before José Fermin dumped a single into right field with one out in the sixth. Eleven of his 20 outs were on groundballs, and he struck out three.</p><p>“That was excellent,” manager Craig Counsell said. “As a sinkerball pitcher that’s what the game looks like when they’re having their day, right? So all the groundballs, the kind of contact.”</p><p>Holmes suffered a broken right fibula in the fourth inning of the Mets’ game against the Yankees at Citi Field when a 111-mph liner off the bat of Spencer Jones struck him on the shin. The righty had several minor league rehab outings in the Mets system before joining the Cubs.</p><p>“It’s one thing to be healthy and it’s another thing to be in your best compete-mode self, and I don’t think that happens overnight,” Counsell said.</p><p>“The first one (rough start) was a little expected almost, but I think what’s so impressive is to see the adjustments that he made so quickly to kind of of get back to being himself."</p><p>Holmes, was a two-time All-Star with the Mets, but as a reliever. He became a starter last season, going 12-8 with a 3.53 ERA for New York.</p><p>His combined record this season is 5-5 with a 2.56 ERA in 11 starts.</p><p>“Coming back from an injury, it’s always a process,” Holmes said. “I probably wasn’t as bad as my stat line last time and probably wasn’t as good as my one this time.</p><p>“In-between starts, there were some simple things that we worked on,” he added. “I think Tommy (Cubs pitching coach Hottovy) really good at communicating things in a simple way, and you know, one or two things we were just trying to nail this week and we were able to do that.”</p><p>Holmes threw 80 pitches this time, 50 for strikes before relievers Ryan Rolison, Ryan Zeferjahn and Jacob Webb finished a three-hitter and the Cubs' fifth shutout win this season. Webb worked around a single in the ninth for his ninth save.</p><p>“It feels like getting the ball on the ground comes natural, Holmes said. "Where I was at today, I was able to make enough pitches to, you know — the slider and sweeper and for the sinker — to create a mix and get people to (hit the ball) on the ground.</p><p>“That’s always a goal for me to try to get a ground ball within three pitches and move on to the next batter.”</p><p>The righty exited to an ovation from the full house of 40,374</p><p>“You know that’s what you imagine, what you kind of hope for when you throw in a Cubs jersey,” Holmes said. “Pitching at Wrigley, Cubs uniform and a Friday day game. It’s special. It’s iconic."</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: New Naismith Hall of Famer Candace Parker still sees reason to believe in the Sky
entries.summary: <p>UNCASVILLE, Conn. — If Candace Parker could thank a body part for making her a Hall of Famer, it would be her brain.</p><p>Parker remembers sitting with her dad at 6 or 7 years old, breaking down defenses.</p><p>In addition to her versatile skill set and physical gifts, Parker's ability to see ahead and read the game made her great.</p><p>Elena Delle Donne, another <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> legend being inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame, could only describe playing against Parker as a “headache.”</p><p>“You had to pressure her because you didn’t want her to see the floor and find her teammates,” she said. “But when you pressure her, she could put it on the floor and go by you.”</p><p>Parker keeps flexing her basketball IQ as an analyst in retirement, now calling WNBA games for Prime Video.</p><p>So it was notable that, when asked about the Sky on Friday, she saw reason for optimism in the 12th-place team. She pointed out that they have already surpassed last year’s win total with 10 games remaining and that their young core has potential.</p><p>“The way they started the season 3-1 — it showed,” she said. “Rickea [Jackson] is that type of player that you can build a franchise around. I think [Kamilla] Cardoso is doing a great job of being dominant in the paint. I think she’s playing better too now that [Courtney] Vandersloot’s back and able to run the show again.”</p><p>Though the season has generally been a disappointment — the Sky <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/08/12/with-playoff-chances-dwindling-time-for-sky-fans-to-look-to-the-future" >will not meet their goal</a> of making the playoffs — Parker has a point. More than either of the previous two seasons, this one has offered flashes of a model that could work.</p><p>There is an argument for giving coach Tyler Marsh, who has spent the season on the hot seat, a chance to run it back with a healthier group.</p><p>The thing about asking Parker to analyze the Sky, though, is that the brain is so deeply connected to the heart.</p><p>She will always have a soft spot for the franchise. She’s a Chicago-area kid who came home and led the Sky to their first championship in 2021.</p><p>She also has a soft spot for Marsh.</p><p>During her time with the Aces, Parker got to know a talented young player-development coach — and universally agreed-upon “great guy” — in Marsh. When Marsh later got the call to become the Sky’s head coach, Parker helped him look over the contract and nudged him to take it.</p><p>So it’s no surprise Parker empathizes with the tough hand he’s been dealt.</p><p>“Things happen you don’t have any control over,” Parker said. “You come in, you have to make a big trade. And then now this season, losing [Jackson to an ACL injury].”</p><p>By “big trade,” Parker was of course referring to the deal that sent three-time All-Star Angel Reese to the Dream right after Marsh had unlocked her as a playmaker.</p><p>The Sky will have a decision to make about Marsh at the end of the season. But their recurring question is bigger than coaching. It is whether the franchise has built the infrastructure needed to cultivate young stars — and keep them.</p><p>Will they be able to develop and retain Jackson? Or will they, as has happened so often, eventually “have to make a big trade”?</p><p>Fortunately for Parker, those questions are not hers to solve.</p><p>She’s accomplished just about all that women’s basketball has to offer: three WNBA championships, two MVPs and two Olympic gold medals. Now, on the eve of her Hall of Fame induction, she gets to look back on it all with a little disbelief.</p><p>“I don’t think anybody picks up a ball like, ‘I’m gonna be a Hall of Famer,’ I’ll be honest,” she said. “But as you start winning and you see that your heroes all have that orange jacket. To be able to get the call and be in this group, it’s cool.”</p><p>Parker said her next project is another heady one: brainwashing her young sons into loving the game enough to chase orange jackets of their own.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Administración de Trump exige a Illinois y otros estados acceso a datos sensibles de conductores de licencias CDL
entries.summary: <p>El fiscal general de Illinois, Kwame Raoul, y más de 20 funcionarios de otros estados demandaron el jueves a la administración de Trump por su exigencia de acceso a las bases de datos estatales que los estados usan para otorgar licencias comerciales de conducir, conocidas como CDL.</p><p>La administración de Trump ha amenazado con recortar más de $10 millones en fondos federales a la Asociación Americana de Administradores de Vehículos Motorizados (AAMVA) por no entregar los últimos cinco años de datos del Sistema de Información de Licencias de Conducir Comerciales.</p><p>La base de datos fue creada a finales de los años 80 para ayudar a los estados a determinar la elegibilidad de los conductores para las CDL entre distintos estados.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-d80000" name="module-d80000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Las demandas sostienen que la administración está violando tanto la ley estatal como la federal al crear su propia versión de la base de datos sin garantías para el manejo de información sensible, como los números de Seguro Social. Las demandas afirman que la administración "no tiene una necesidad legítima de adueñarse de esta base de datos de registros estatales, y no consultó a los estados antes de realizar este cambio drástico".</p><p>El Departamento de Transporte de Estados Unidos no respondió de inmediato a una solicitud de comentarios.</p><p>Según la demanda, la base de datos incluye nombres de conductores, fechas de nacimiento, números de Seguro Social, números de licencia de conducir y el nombre de los estados que proporcionaron el registro, y pertenece a los estados que la crean. Si la corte falla a favor del gobierno federal, la información de más de 17 millones de conductores sería compartida con la administración de Trump.</p><p>Además, las leyes estatales de Illinois y California exigen permiso por escrito de cada estado para que la AAMVA comparta la información que ha recopilado de los estados, según la demanda.</p><p>El secretario de Estado de Illinois, Alexi Giannoulias, cuyo departamento se encarga de velar por el cumplimiento de la privacidad de los datos de los registros de Illinois compartidos en la base de datos, dijo que el gobierno federal estaba exigiendo una "cantidad sin precedentes de información personal sensible propiedad del estado" sin "justificación legal adecuada".</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: Amtrak's funding boost paves way for White Sox chairman-in-waiting Justin Ishbia's South Loop vision
entries.summary: <p>More than $600 million in federal grants announced Friday will help Amtrak relocate its Chicago maintenance facility from the South Loop to Bridgeport, paving the way for a new mega-development backed by potential White Sox chairman-in-waiting Justin Ishbia that could eventually grow to include a new stadium.</p><p>Amtrak is putting most of its newly awarded Federal Railroad Administration funding toward a new Midwest Maintenance Facility at the current site of a Union Pacific rail yard in Bridgeport, according to an Amtrak statement.</p><p>That’ll open up Amtrak’s current 47-acre site along the Chicago River south of Roosevelt Road, which Ishbia’s private equity firm, Shore Capital Partners, is under contract to purchase. The firm <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/03/18/justin-ishbia-stadium-white-sox-the-78-amtrak" target="_blank" ><u>announced plans in March</u></a> for a mixed-use development including a medical campus in partnership with Northwestern Medicine.</p><p>But sources close to the sprawling proposal have said Ishbia has also considered a future Sox stadium at the site, which is on the west side the river just across from The 78, where current Sox chairman Jerry Reinsdorf covets a new stadium.</p><p>Reinsdorf has lobbied state lawmakers to no avail for public funding at The 78, where the Chicago Fire broke ground earlier this year on a new stadium fully funded by billionaire owner Joe Mansueto, though it relies on <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/06/17/mayor-brandon-johnson-425m-tif-subsidy-the-78" target="_blank" ><u>$425 million in tax-increment financing</u></a> district funding for infrastructure improvements.</p><p>The Sox announced <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2025/06/05/white-sox-jerry-reinsdorf-justin-ishbia-ownership-transfer-new-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>a potential succession plan last year</u></a> that would give Ishbia the option to buy a controlling interest in the Sox from Reinsdorf as early as 2029, the year the team’s lease is up at publicly owned Rate Field.</p><p>Until that happens, Ishbia has emphasized that all Sox decisions lie with Reinsdorf. Other rail yards will have to change hands for any stadium vision to come to fruition on the west bank of the river.</p><p>Ishbia has pumped more than $125 million into Canal Edge LLC, the entity financing and delivering the new $900 million Amtrak facility in Bridgeport, where work is expected to start this fall and last for 18 months.</p><p>“Canal Edge is proud to partner with Amtrak and take responsibility for delivering this critical investment in Chicago’s rail infrastructure,” Ishbia said in a statement provided by Amtrak. “By committing substantial private capital and standing behind the delivery of this project, we are investing in the South Side, creating union jobs, and building infrastructure that will strengthen Chicago and the national rail network for generations.”</p><p>Ishbia has all but guaranteed a new stadium at some point if he obtains control of the team, telling the Sun-Times <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/pope-leo-xiv/2025/11/19/justin-ishbia-pope-white-sox-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>last fall</u></a> that “whether a new stadium occurs in four years or 34 years, I don’t know, but I’m going to be involved in a stadium at some point with the White Sox.”</p><p>U.S. Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Illinois, said his state’s share of some $5.3 billion in federal rail funding “reflects the city’s status as a thriving transportation hub.”</p><p>Amtrak’s new rail yard “will allow for more efficient servicing of rail cars, reduce service disruptions and turnaround time,” according to the agency, which said its current facilities “were designed for a different era and no longer provide the space, configuration, or modern capabilities needed to support today’s fleet or anticipated future growth.”</p><p>Amtrak is hosting a community meeting on the new rail yard project Aug. 26 at 5:30 p.m. at the Pui Tak Center, 2218 S. Wentworth Ave.</p>
